subject: chemistry

moments.title: Latimer and Rodebush
moments.body: Two Berkeley graduate students propose the 'hydrogen bond' to explain anomalous properties of water and HF. The paper is rejected by their advisor G. N. Lewis, who later publishes the idea.
moments.takeaway: The hydrogen bond is named, then nearly suppressed by an advisor.

moments.title: Pauling formalises
moments.body: In 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond', Pauling gives the hydrogen bond its modern framework. He proposes it underlies water's unique behaviour, protein structure, and DNA pairing (later).
moments.takeaway: H-bonding becomes a central concept across chemistry and biology.

moments.title: DNA base pairing
moments.body: Watson-Crick base pairing — A-T, G-C — relies on hydrogen bonds. Without H-bonds, DNA cannot replicate. Heredity rests on this weakest of bonds.

moments.title: H-bonding in catalysis
moments.body: Hydrogen-bond donors (thioureas, squaramides) catalyse asymmetric reactions. Bonds 'too weak to matter' make industrial-scale enantioselectivity.
moments.takeaway: Hydrogen bonds are the workhorse of modern asymmetric catalysis.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Hydrogen bonding explains water's anomalies, protein folding, DNA replication, sapphire's hardness, and asymmetric catalysis. It is omnipresent in chemistry teaching.
now.open_questions: What is the limit of hydrogen-bond strength? Can engineered H-bond networks rival covalent bonds in toughness?

reflection: Lewis suppressed his students' hydrogen-bond paper before publishing the idea. How often does priority disputes obscure credit?
